```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_xgboost = requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)
has_python  = requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE) && reticulate::py_available(initialize = TRUE)
has_sklearn = has_python && reticulate::py_module_available("sklearn")
has_catenc  = has_python && reticulate::py_module_available("category_encoders")
has_pylmnn  = has_python && reticulate::py_module_available("pylmnn")
has_fastdummies = requireNamespace("fastDummies", quietly = TRUE)
has_smbinning   = requireNamespace("smbinning", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette walks through every transformer class in rml, family by family. Each section explains
what the transformer does, lists the arguments specific to it, and shows it on its own and inside a
model. Arguments shared by all models (`name`, `features.include`, `features.exclude`, `verbose`, and so
on) are described in `vignette('rml-reference')` and in `?MODEL`. Models with transformers print their
progress while fitting; the examples set `verbose = 0` to keep the output short.

A transformer is an ordinary model: it has `fit(X, y)` and `predict(X)`. Used alone, `predict()`
returns its output columns. Used inside another model's `transformers` list, its output columns become
that model's input features (see `vignette('rml-pipelines')`).

Class names follow the pattern `<TYPE>.<PACKAGE>.<ALGORITHM>`: `ENC.RML.TE` is an encoder (`ENC`)
implemented in rml (`RML`) doing target encoding (`TE`).

## Data used in the examples

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(rml)
set.seed(42)
n = 2000
X = data.frame(
  age     = round(runif(n, 18, 80)),
  income  = round(rlnorm(n, 10, 0.6)),
  balance = rnorm(n, 5000, 2000),
  visits  = rpois(n, 3),
  region  = sample(c('north', 'south', 'east', 'west'), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.4, .3, .2, .1)),
  channel = sample(c('web', 'branch', 'phone'), n, replace = TRUE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
logit = -1 + 0.03*(X$age - 45) + 0.8*(log(X$income) - 10) + 0.0003*(X$balance - 5000) +
        c(north = 0.8, south = -0.5, east = 0.2, west = -1)[X$region] + 0.6*(X$channel == 'web')
y = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(logit))
train = sample(n, 1500)
Xtr = X[train, ];  ytr = y[train]
Xte = X[-train, ]; yte = y[-train]
gini = function(model) model$performance(Xte, yte, metrics = 'gini')
```

`X` has four numeric columns (`age`, `income`, `balance`, `visits`) and two categorical columns
(`region`, `channel`). The binary target depends on all of them.

## Encoders: categorical columns to numbers

Encoders read the categorical columns (character, factor, and for some encoders integer) and output
numeric columns. Numeric columns are ignored.

### ENC.RML.TE: target encoder

Replaces each categorical column by the share of class 1 among training rows with the same value.
Values not seen in training get the median rate. It has no specific arguments.

```{r te}
te = ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te', features.include = c('region', 'channel'))
te$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(te$predict(Xte), 3)
```

Target encoding feeds a logistic regression with one number per categorical column instead of one
column per value:

```{r te-model}
lr_te = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr_te', verbose = 0, transformers = list(
  te, MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'num', features.include = c('age', 'income', 'balance', 'visits'))))
lr_te$fit(Xtr, ytr)
gini(lr_te)
```

### ENC.RML.FE: numeric aggregates per category

For each categorical column and each numeric column, outputs the aggregate of the numeric column
within the row's category, for example the mean income per region.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `aggregator` | Name of the aggregate function | `'mean'` |
| `categoricals` | Categorical columns to use | all |
| `action_by_original` | Function of (aggregate, original value) applied to each output, e.g. a difference | none |

```{r fe}
fe = ENC.RML.FE(name = 'fe', features.include = c('region', 'income', 'age'))
fe$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(fe$predict(Xte), 3)
```

### ENC.RML.ME and ENC.RML.MEB: one model per category

`ENC.RML.ME` fits a separate model on the rows of each category value with enough rows, plus a global
model on all rows. Each row is scored by its category's model, or the global one. The output is one
column per categorical column. `ENC.RML.MEB` holds out 30% of the training rows and keeps a category's
model only if it beats the global model there.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model.class` | Class of the segment models | `'CLS.STATS.LR'` |
| `model.config` | `list` of arguments of the segment models | `list()` |
| `min_rows` | Minimum rows for a category to get its own model | 100 |
| `segmentation_features` | Categorical columns to segment by | all |

```{r me}
me = ENC.RML.ME(name = 'me', model.class = 'CLS.STATS.LR', min_rows = 150,
                features.include = c('region', 'age', 'income', 'balance'))
me$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(me$predict(Xte), 3)
```

### One-hot encoders

`ENC.SKLEARN.OHE` (scikit-learn) and `ENC.FASTDUMMIES.OHE` (package fastDummies) create one 0/1 column
per value. Both take `max_domain` (default 25): columns with more distinct values are not encoded.
`ENC.SKLEARN.OHE` names its outputs `<column>_<value>` and gives all-zero rows for values not seen in
training.

```{r ohe-sk, eval = has_sklearn}
ohe = ENC.SKLEARN.OHE(name = 'ohe', features.include = c('region', 'channel'))
ohe$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(ohe$predict(Xte), 3)
```

```{r ohe-fd, eval = has_fastdummies}
ohe2 = ENC.FASTDUMMIES.OHE(name = 'dummies', features.include = c('region', 'channel'))
ohe2$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(ohe2$predict(Xte), 3)
```

### category_encoders

`ENC.CATEGORY_ENCODERS.TE` (target), `.CATB` (CatBoost), `.JSTN` (James-Stein) and `.HLMRT` (Helmert)
wrap the encoders of the Python package category_encoders. Arguments other than rml's own are passed to
the Python encoder.

```{r catenc, eval = has_catenc}
cb = ENC.CATEGORY_ENCODERS.CATB(name = 'catb', features.include = c('region', 'channel'))
cb$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(cb$predict(Xte), 3)
```

### CATCONCATER: combined category

Outputs one column joining the categorical values of a row with `'-'`, for example `north-web`. Feed it
to a target encoder to encode combinations of categories:

```{r concat}
combo = ENC.RML.TE(name = 'combo_te', verbose = 0, transformers = list(
  CATCONCATER(name = 'combo', features.include = c('region', 'channel'))))
combo$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(combo$predict(Xte), 3)
```

## Mappers: one output column per input column

Mappers transform numeric columns one to one, or project them to a smaller set.

| Class | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `MAP.RML.IDT` | The input columns unchanged |
| `MAP.RML.MMS` | `(x - min)/(max - min)` with training min and max |
| `MAP.RML.ZFS` | `(x - mean)/sd` with training mean and sd |
| `MAP.SKLEARN.MMS`, `MAP.SKLEARN.ZFS`, `MAP.SKLEARN.NRM`, `MAP.SKLEARN.QT` | scikit-learn's `MinMaxScaler`, `StandardScaler`, `Normalizer`, `QuantileTransformer` |
| `MAP.STATS.PCA` | First principal components (`num_components`, default 5; `center`, `scale`) |
| `MAP.PYLMNN.LMNN` | Large margin nearest neighbour projection (`num_components`, `num_neighbors`, `epochs`) |

`MAP.RML.IDT` is the way to give a model raw columns next to the outputs of other transformers. The
scalers map missing and undefined values to 0.

```{r mappers}
num = c('age', 'income', 'balance', 'visits')
zfs = MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', features.include = num)
zfs$fit(Xtr)
round(sapply(zfs$predict(Xte), function(v) c(mean = mean(v), sd = sd(v))), 2)

mms = MAP.RML.MMS(name = 'mm', features.include = num)
mms$fit(Xtr)
round(sapply(mms$predict(Xte), range), 2)

pca = MAP.STATS.PCA(name = 'pca', num_components = 2, features.include = num)
pca$fit(Xtr)
head(pca$predict(Xte), 3)
```

```{r mappers-sk, eval = has_sklearn}
qt = MAP.SKLEARN.QT(name = 'qt', n_quantiles = 100L, output_distribution = 'normal', features.include = num)
qt$fit(Xtr)
head(qt$predict(Xte), 3)
```

```{r lmnn, eval = has_pylmnn}
lmnn = MAP.PYLMNN.LMNN(name = 'lmnn', num_components = 2, features.include = num)
lmnn$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(lmnn$predict(Xte), 3)
```

## Binners and clustering

Binners cut numeric columns into bins; clustering binners assign each row to a cluster.

### BIN.RML.OBB: optimal binary binner

Splits each numeric column at the cut point with the strongest chi-square association with the binary
target, and returns 0/1 per column. The importance in its feature table is the strength of that split.

```{r obb}
obb = BIN.RML.OBB(name = 'obb', features.include = num)
obb$fit(Xtr, ytr)
obb$objects$model[c('Column', 'split')]
head(obb$predict(Xte), 3)
```

### BIN.SMBINNING.OB: optimal binning with smbinning

Bins each numeric column with `smbinning::smbinning` (conditional inference trees) into a categorical
column. `percentageOfRecords` (default 0.05) is the minimum share of rows per bin. Column names must not
contain dots.

```{r smb, eval = has_smbinning}
smb = BIN.SMBINNING.OB(name = 'smb', features.include = c('age', 'income'))
smb$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(smb$predict(Xte), 3)
```

### BIN.RML.GROUPER: grouping categories

Groups the values of each categorical column by their target rate, so that values with similar rates
share a group. `encoding = 'target_ratio'` (default) clusters the rates and picks the number of groups
with a chi-square test.

```{r grouper}
grp = BIN.RML.GROUPER(name = 'grp', features.include = 'region')
grp$fit(Xtr, ytr)
unique(cbind(Xte['region'], group = grp$predict(Xte)[[1]]))
```

### Clustering: BIN.KMEANS.KMC and BIN.SKLEARN.KMC

Both cluster the rows on the numeric columns with k-means and return the cluster number of each row
(the nearest centre for new rows). `BIN.KMEANS.KMC` uses `stats::kmeans` with `num_clusters` (default
5); `BIN.SKLEARN.KMC` uses scikit-learn's `KMeans` with `n_clusters` (default 3). Scale the columns first,
otherwise the column with the largest range dominates the distances:

```{r kmeans}
km = BIN.KMEANS.KMC(name = 'km', verbose = 0, num_clusters = 4, transformers = list(
  MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', features.include = num)))
km$fit(Xtr)
table(km$predict(Xte)[[1]])
```

A cluster number is a category, so a target encoder can turn it into a feature:

```{r kmeans-te}
cluster_te = ENC.RML.TE(name = 'cluster_rate', verbose = 0, transformers = list(km))
cluster_te$fit(Xtr, ytr)
head(cluster_te$predict(Xte), 3)
```

```{r kmeans-sk, eval = has_sklearn}
skm = BIN.SKLEARN.KMC(name = 'skm', verbose = 0, n_clusters = 4, transformers = list(
  MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', features.include = num)))
skm$fit(Xtr)
table(skm$predict(Xte)[[1]])
```

The functions `elbow()`, `best_num_clusters()` and `cluster_tree()` help choose the number of clusters;
see `vignette('rml-ensembles-and-tools')`.

## Feature generators

| Class | Output |
| --- | --- |
| `FET.RML.D2MUL` | Product of every pair of numeric columns, named `<a>_X_<b>` |
| `FET.SKLEARN.MFG` | scikit-learn's `PolynomialFeatures` (`degree`, `interaction_only`, ...) |

```{r d2mul}
d2 = FET.RML.D2MUL(name = 'd2', features.include = c('age', 'visits', 'balance'))
d2$fit(Xtr)
head(d2$predict(Xte), 3)
```

```{r mfg, eval = has_sklearn}
mfg = FET.SKLEARN.MFG(name = 'poly', degree = 2L, interaction_only = TRUE, include_bias = FALSE,
                      features.include = c('age', 'visits'))
mfg$fit(Xtr)
head(mfg$predict(Xte), 3)
```

## Function transformers

Function transformers apply a fixed function to each numeric column.

| Class | Output | Arguments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FNT.RML.LOG` | `log(x + intercept)` | `intercept` (1), `apply_abs` (TRUE: use `abs(x)`) |
| `FNT.RML.INV` | `1/x`, limited to `trim` | `trim` (10000) |
| `FNT.RML.LOGIT` | logit of x, after min-max scaling to [0, 1] | `apply_mms` (TRUE) |
| `FNT.RML.POLY` | `v, v^2, ..., v^n_terms` with `v = gain*x + intercept`, named `<column>_T<k>` | `n_terms` (3), `gain` (1), `intercept` (0), `apply_abs` (FALSE) |

```{r fnt}
lg = FNT.RML.LOG(name = 'log', features.include = 'income')
lg$fit(Xtr); head(lg$predict(Xte), 3)

inv = FNT.RML.INV(name = 'inv', features.include = 'visits')
inv$fit(Xtr); head(inv$predict(Xte), 3)

pl = FNT.RML.POLY(name = 'poly', n_terms = 3, gain = 1/50, features.include = 'age')
pl$fit(Xtr); head(pl$predict(Xte), 3)

lt = FNT.RML.LOGIT(name = 'logit', features.include = 'balance')
lt$fit(Xtr); head(lt$predict(Xte), 3)
```

## Putting it together

A logistic regression whose features are the log of income, polynomial terms of age, the scaled
balance and target-encoded categories, compared with the same regression on the raw numeric columns:

```{r together}
raw = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'raw', features.include = num)
engineered = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'engineered', verbose = 0, transformers = list(
  FNT.RML.LOG(name = 'log', features.include = 'income'),
  FNT.RML.POLY(name = 'age', n_terms = 2, gain = 1/50, features.include = 'age'),
  MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', features.include = c('balance', 'visits')),
  ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te', features.include = c('region', 'channel'))))
raw$fit(Xtr, ytr)
engineered$fit(Xtr, ytr)
c(raw = gini(raw), engineered = gini(engineered))
```

The fitted network can be listed with `info.transformers()`:

```{r info}
engineered$info.transformers()[c('name', 'class', 'type')]
```

## Writing your own transformer

A transformer is a class that inherits from `MODEL` and implements `model.fit(X, y)` and
`model.predict(X)`. `X` in `model.fit` holds only the columns the model may use; set
`objects$features` to the subset it really uses, so that `predict` passes those columns.
`model.predict` returns a `data.frame`; its column names become `<name>_<column>`.

```{r custom}
MAP.RML.RANK = setRefClass('MAP.RML.RANK', contains = 'MODEL', methods = list(
  initialize = function(...){
    callSuper(...)
    type <<- 'Mapper'; description <<- 'Rank of each value among training values (0 to 1)'
    package <<- 'rml'; package_language <<- 'R'
    if(is.empty(name)){name <<- 'RNK' %>% paste0(sample(10000:99999, 1))}
  },
  model.fit = function(X, y = NULL){
    objects$features <<- objects$features %>% filter(fclass %in% c('numeric', 'integer'))
    objects$model <<- lapply(X[objects$features$fname], function(v) sort(v))
  },
  model.predict = function(X){
    out = mapply(function(v, ref) findInterval(v, ref)/length(ref), X[objects$features$fname], objects$model)
    as.data.frame(matrix(out, nrow = nrow(X), dimnames = list(NULL, objects$features$fname)))
  }
))
rk = MAP.RML.RANK(name = 'rank', features.include = c('income', 'balance'))
rk$fit(Xtr)
head(rk$predict(Xte), 3)
```
